text:
Probably yes, if closing costs are under about $8-9k.

On a fresh 30-year term, the payment drops from about $2,528 to $2,373, saving roughly $155/month. Over your 10 years that's about $18,700. Refinance costs typically run 2-3% of the loan ($8-12k), so the break-even looks like this:

| Closing costs | Break-even |
|---|---|
| $6k | ~3 years |
| $8k | ~4.3 years |
| $10k | ~5.4 years |
| $12k | ~6.4 years |

At a 10-year horizon, you net roughly $7-12k in the good cases and close to zero at the high end of costs. A 0.6-point drop is on the thin side, so the deal depends almost entirely on the fees.

Three things can change the answer:

- **Remaining term.** If you're several years into the current loan, a new 30-year term resets your amortization. Part of the lower payment is just a longer schedule. To keep the benefit, ask for a 25- or 20-year term, or keep paying the old amount, which would pay the new loan off sooner.
- **Rolling costs into the loan.** This hides the break-even but you pay interest on the fees. Compare using the actual cash out of pocket.
- **Possible further rate drops.** If rates fall again, you can refinance a second time, but each round costs fees again. Rolling the cost into a lender credit (a slightly higher rate, no closing costs) makes repeat refinancing cheap, and is worth quoting.

Get Loan Estimates from 3 lenders, since fees vary a lot. If the all-in cost comes in under about $8k, do it.
